name: Vivid violet
lede: Vivid violet is an intensity modifier of plain [[violet]], pushed to one of the most saturated purples in ColorHub's graph, and the family also carries a brighter twin of Rebecca Purple.

sections.title: A pushed-up violet
sections.body:
ColorHub's graph lists Vivid violet as a modifier built from the base color [[violet]], its listed parent, the same grammar that produces Dark violet or Deep violet from the same root hue [1]. The hex #8601AF measures a vivid purple by ISCC-NBS, a very close match at only 3.0 units from its nearest block, close to 4.1P 3.4/19.2 in Munsell notation, with a chroma of 97 out of 100, near the top of what the color space can represent at this lightness [2]. Among its nearby library entries is *Vivid rebecca purple*, a brighter, more saturated sibling of [[rebecca-purple]] built the same way [1]. No single coiner or date is recorded for "vivid violet" itself, since an intensity word plus a base hue is a label anyone could apply [1].

Other "vivid" relatives in our data occupy the same high-chroma end of their own base hues, including [[vivid-lilac|Vivid lilac]] where it exists, each one testing how far a hue can be pushed before it reads as a different color altogether [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive carries a close match to Vivid violet covering at least one percent of its canvas, as photographed [3]. That gap fits the color's own chroma value, 97 out of 100: pigments this saturated in violet were rare and unstable before synthetic dyes arrived in the nineteenth century, so a true match would be unusual in an archive weighted toward earlier painting [3]. In printed English the phrase rises fastest in the 1870s and peaks in the 2010s, consistent with a descriptive compound that drifted in and out of use rather than one tied to a single event [4].
